contenido: 1. Since the fundamental concern of the Church is to announce and promote faith in the society of our time, subject to profound socio-cultural transformations, it is convenient—keeping in mind what the Second Vatican Council has stated—to describe some specific features of the current situation, indicating the spiritual repercussions and the new commitments that this situation places before the Church.

2. "Today the human race finds itself in a new period of its history, characterized by profound and accelerated changes, which progressively extend to the entire Universe... We can now speak of a true social and cultural transformation that is also reflected in religious life" (GS. 4).

3. "For all this, the changes experienced by traditional local communities, such as the patriarchal family, the clan, the tribe, the village, other different groups and the same relationships of social coexistence, are becoming more profound every day" (GS. 6).

4. The construction of human society, progress and the gradual realization of human projects mobilize the energies of the men of our time (GS. 4). Faith cannot remain alien to these progresses which, on the other hand, can be accompanied by serious deviations. The evangelical message must provide its judgment on this state of affairs and show men the meaning of these events.
5. Scientific, technical, industrial and urban civilization not infrequently removes man's interest in divine things and makes it more difficult for him to have inner concern for religious life.

6. The Christian faith of many faithful is in serious danger, especially in those places where religion was considered the prerogative of some social classes, or where that faith relied too much on ancient customs and the unanimity of the religious profession.

7. Many baptized people have distanced themselves from religion in such a way that they come to profess, in a certain indifferentism and disguise, even atheism. "There are many, however, who today ignore the meaning of this intimate and vital union with God and explicitly deny it. This atheism is one of the most serious phenomena of our time. And it must be examined with all attention" (GS. 19).

8. There is also no shortage of Christians, especially among those who have received a higher cultural training, who experience a certain discontent with the language of faith that they judge to be too attached to outdated formulas and Western culture.

9. In this situation of such profound changes, anyone could think that the apostolic effort that the Church intends to deploy is useless. In reality, one cannot accuse the zeal of the pastors or that of the faithful, which is truly great. The impediments to more effective action seem to come either from the lack of adequate preparation for the new and difficult commitments offered to the ministry of the word or from a still imperfect reflection that is expressed in theories that, far from favoring, hinder the evangelical initiative.

10. In the DV. Constitution, the Ecumenical Council considers revelation as an act through which God enters into communion with us personally: "God, in his goodness and wisdom, wanted to reveal himself and manifest the mystery of will..., to invite you and receive you into his company (a todos los hombres)" (DV. 2). Thus God appears as someone who wants to communicate himself, carrying out a project inspired by love.

11. God, to make his plan known to men, works through the events of salvation history and through inspired words that accompany and clarify these events: "Revelation is carried out with facts and words intrinsically linked; the works that God performs in the history of salvation manifest and confirm the doctrine and realities that the words signify; in turn, the words proclaim the works and explain their mystery" (DV. 2).
12. "The profound truth of God and of the salvation of man that this revelation transmits..., shines in Christ, mediator and fullness of all revelation" (DV. 2).

13. "That is why the Apostles, when transmitting what they wrote, warn the faithful to preserve the traditions learned by word or by letter. What the apostles transmitted includes everything necessary for a holy life and for a growing faith of the people of God; thus the Church with its teaching, its life, its worship, preserves and 'transmits to all ages what it is and what it believes' (DV. 8),

14. Divine revelation, by special inspiration of the Holy Spirit, has also been expressed in written form, that is, in the Sacred Books of the Old and New Testament, which contain and present the truth revealed by God (Cfr. DV. 11).
15. With faith, man receives revelation and through it consciously participates in God's gift.

16. The ministry of the Word, to put it briefly, must be aware of the task entrusted to it, that is, to raise a living faith that converts the mind to God, encourages assent to his action and leads to a living knowledge of the contents of the tradition and reveals and manifests the true meaning of the world and human existence.
17. The ministry of the word takes different forms, according to the different ways of exercising it and the purposes pursued, among them is catechesis.

18. Catechesis in itself presupposes a global adherence to the Gospel of Christ, proposed by the Church. However, it is sometimes addressed to men who, although they belong to the Church, never in fact had a true personal adherence to the revealed message.
19. Catechesis necessarily takes various forms depending on the circumstances and needs of the case.
20. Pastors should remember their duty to promote and ensure the illustration of the Christian life by the word of God, according to age and circumstances (CD,
21. In pastoral activity, catechesis is a form of ecclesial action that seeks to bring both communities and individuals to maturity of faith.

22. Faith is a gift from God that causes the conversion of man. "To give this response of faith, the grace of God is necessary, which comes forward and helps us, together with the help of the Holy Spirit, who moves the heart, directs it to God, opens the eyes of the Spirit and grants everyone the pleasure to accept and believe the truth" (DV, 5).

24. The mature man in faith knows the mystery of salvation revealed in Christ and the miracles and divine facts that prove that this mystery is realized in human history. Therefore, it is not enough for catechesis to excite only a religious experience, even if it is true, but it must lead to gradually perceiving the entire truth of the divine plan, teaching the faithful to read the Holy Scriptures and know the tradition.

25. "Every liturgical celebration, through the work of Christ the Priest and his body, which is the Church, is a sacred action par excellence whose effectiveness, with the same title and to the same degree, is not equaled by any other action of the Church" (SC, 7). But the Christian community, the more it matures in faith, lives worship in spirit and in truth mainly in the Eucharistic liturgical celebrations (Jn, 4,23).
26. The man who is already mature in faith can recognize in different circumstances and encounters with his neighbor the invitation of God that calls him to embrace his plan of salvation.
27. The communities of the faithful, depending on the circumstances, must participate in ecumenical dialogue and in other projects relating to the restoration of Christian unity (tJR. 5).

28. The Church in 'Christ is like the sacrament or the sign and the instrument of salvation and unity of all humanity (LG. 1). And in this sense it is 'all the more visible the more mature in faith the communities of the faithful appear,
29. The mature man in faith directs his thoughts and desires to the full consummation of the Kingdom in eternal life.

30. In the faithful, faith appears more or less developed according to the grace that the Holy Spirit gives to each one and which must be obtained through constant prayer, and according to the response that each person gives to that grace (Mr. 9,23).

31. Catechesis is directed at the community without forgetting the faithful in particular. It joins the other pastoral activities of the Church but retains its specific nature, and fulfills at the same time its duty of initiation, education and teaching.
32. Remember in catechesis that expression from Holy Scripture: "Living and effective is the word of God" (Heb. 4,12).

33. God in the History of Revelation used a pedagogy to announce in the O.T. his plans of salvation through prophecies and figures that prepare the coming of his. Son, author and perfecter of the Faith in the N. T. (Hebr. 12,2).

34. Catechesis remains faithful to the word of God and its expression (DV. 24). Drawing out the truth of the word of God, with full adherence to the sure expression of this word, catechesis attempts to teach the word of God with complete fidelity.

35. Catechesis finally asks, both from catechists and from the ecclesial community, the testimony of faith accompanied by the example of an authentic Christian life and the capacity for sacrifice (16. 12,17; NA. 2).

36. The faith whose maturation catechesis seeks (n. 21), can be considered in two ways: as man's full adhesion to God who reveals himself, under the influence of grace (fides qua), or as the matter of revelation and the Christian message (fides quae).

37. Revelation is the manifestation of the mystery of God and his saving action in history, made by God himself to man through a personal communication, the content of which He wants to be preached to all men as a message of salvation.

38. The material of the message of salvation consists of parts closely linked together, even though its revelation was made progressively by God, first by the prophets and ultimately through his Son (H-ebr, 1.1).

39. - The object of faith is - by its nature complex, that is: God in his mystery and his saving intervention in history, and we know this from what God himself has revealed about himself and his works. -

40. Christ Jesus, the incarnate Word of God, being the supreme way in which God intervenes in the world and manifests himself to men, is the center of the evangelical message in the History of salvation.

41. Just as Christ is the center of the history of salvation, so the mystery of God is the center from which this history begins and towards which it is ordered as the ultimate goal. The dead and risen Christ leads men to the Father by sending the Holy Spirit to the People of God. For this reason the structure of all catechesis must be theocentric — trinitarian: through Christ to the Father in the Spirit.

42. The theocentric-Trinitarian goal of the economy of salvation cannot be separated from its object, which consists in men freed from sin and its consequences being configured as much as possible to Christ (Cfr. LG. 39). Like the Incarnation of the Word, so, all the truth revealed is for us men and for our salvation. The prospective relationship of all Christian truths with the ultimate end of man is one of the conditions for his profitable intelligence (Con. Vat. 1. Const. Dei Filius, Dz. Sch., 3016).

referencias.descripcion: Con. Vat. 1. Const. Dei Filius, Dz. Sch., 3016

contenido: 43. In the message of salvation there is a certain hierarchy of truths (tJR. 11), which the Church has always recognized, when developing the symbols or compendia of the truths of the faith. This
44. The economy of salvation is carried out in time:

45. The content of catechesis is found in the written Word of God or in tradition; The believing people understand it and explain it more deeply under the direction of the Magisterium, which is the only one that teaches authentically; we celebrated it was the liturgy; It shines in the Church, mainly in the righteous and in the saints; and in some way it becomes evident in the same moral values ​​that, by God's providence, exist in human society.

46. The norms indicated above that refer to the exposition of the subject matter of catechesis must be applied in the various forms of catechesis: that is, in biblical and liturgical catechesis, in the doctrinal compendium, in the interpretation of the concrete conditions of human existence, etc.

47. The history of salvation is the same as the history of the means and ways in which the one and true God: Father, Son, Holy Spirit, reveals himself to men, whom, separated from sin, he reconciles and unites with himself.

48. "The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Efe. 1,3) is "a living God" (Mt. 16, 16): holy, just, merciful, he is a God who is the author of an alliance with men, God who sees, liberates, saves, God who loves as a Father, as a husband. Catechesis announces this God with joy, as the source of all hope (1 Petr. 1, 3-4),

49. Christians can help the atheist world to draw closer to God, through the testimony of their lives in accordance with the message of charity of Christ and of living and mature faith that is manifested in works of justice and love (GS. 21).

50. The crowning of all the works of God is the Incarnation of his Son Jesus Christ. Firstborn of all creation, He has being before all things and all things have their consistency in Him (Col. 1, 15-17). In Him, through Him, and for Him all things were created (Col. 1, 15 ss). -
51. The world created from nothing is the world in which, in reality, salvation and redemption through Jesus Christ take place.

52. In Jesus Christ the Christian knows himself to be united to all of history and in communion with all men. In the middle of the history of the world, the history of salvation takes place in which God carries out his plan, so that the people of God or the "total Christ" can be made in time.

53. This great mystery, Christ the Head and Lord of all things "became visible to men by becoming incarnate" (1 Tim. 3, 16). The man Christ Jesus who lived among men, worked with the hands of a man, thought with the intelligence of a man, acted with the will of a man, loved with the heart of a man, is truly the Word and the Son of God who through the Incarnation was united in a certain way with each of the men.
54. The mystery of Christ appears in the history of men in the world, subject to sin, not only as a mystery of Incarnation, but of Salvation and Redemption.

55. The mystery of Christ continues in the Church that always enjoys his presence and serves him, through the signs instituted by Christ himself to signify and confer grace, and are properly called sacraments (Conc. Tridentinum, Decretum de sacramentis, Dz. - Sch., 1601).

referencias.descripcion: Conc. Tridentinum, Decretum de sacramentis, Dz. - Sch., 1601

contenido: 56. Care of catechesis is to propose the sacraments according to their integral nature.

57. Baptism cleanses man of original guilt and all personal sin, makes him a child of God, incorporates him into the Church and sanctifies him with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and, by an indelible character impressed on his soul, makes him an initial participant in the prophetic, royal and priestly mission of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Petr. 29; LG. 31).
58. Without a doubt the Eucharist has primacy over all the sacraments, and the greatest effectiveness in the edification of the Church (LG. 11, 17; Instr. Eucharisticum mysterium, nn 5-15).

59. Today—with the due respect that the Christian message has for consecrated virginity—(1. Cor. 7,38; Concilium Tridentinum, Canones de sacramento matrimonii, Dz. - Sch., 1810), we must give particular importance to the catechesis on marriage instituted by the Creator himself and enriched with various goods, purposes and laws (Gs. 48).

referencias.descripcion: 1. Cor. 7,38; Concilium Tridentinum, Canones de sacramento matrimonii, Dz. - Sch., 1810

contenido: 60. By receiving the Spirit of Christ, man begins a completely new and free way of life with God.
61. Man's divine vocation asks of him a free response in Jesus Christ.
62. Historical and environmental conditions are not, however, the main obstacle to man's freedom: the greatest obstacle that man has to freely adhere to the work of salvation is sin.

63. Christ entrusted his apostles with the task of teaching to observe all the things that he had taught (Mt. 28,20). That is why catechesis does not only include the truths that must be believed but also the things that must be done.

64. The action of the Spirit of Christ is well expressed when the originality of Christian morality is brought to light, which consists of summarizing and centering all ethical commitment, precepts and advice, in that element that is like its soul, that is, in a faith that works in charity (Gal. 5,6).

65. The Church established by Christ was born from his death and Resurrection. She is the new People of God, prepared in the History of Israel, a people that Christ vivifies and makes grow with the outpouring of his spirit and that he continually renews and directs with his hierarchical and charismatic gifts; "people gathered in the unity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit" (LG. 4).
66. The Church is a communion; She has acquired a renewed awareness of this truth in the Second Vatican Council. -

67. The Church is presented not only as a communion of brothers who have Christ as their head, but also as an institution to which a universal saving mission has been entrusted. The People of God "instituted by Christ to be a communion of life, charity and truth, also uses it as an instrument of universal redemption and sends it to the entire universe as the light of the world and salt of the earth" (LG. 9), -
68. Ineffably united to the Lord is Mary, always Virgin, his Mother who "occupies in the Holy Church, after Christ, the highest position and the closest to us" (LG. 54).

69. In Jesus Christ and through his mystery, believers wait with hope from this earthly life "for our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transfigure our humble body to conform it to his glorious body" (Fil. 3,21; 1 Cor. 15). -

70. In this century, catechists have deepened the methodological problems presented by the psychological, didactic and pedagogical sciences. For in truth the study of the method of the catechism lesson has been undertaken; the role of active methods in catechesis has been clarified; The catechetical act has been analyzed according to the laws of learning (la experiencia, la imaginación, la memoria, la inteligencia); A differential methodology has been developed according to ages, social environments, and the degree of psychic development of the subject.

referencias.descripcion: la experiencia, la imaginación, la memoria, la inteligencia

contenido: 71. No methodology, no matter how experienced, will exempt the catechist from a personal effort to assimilate and adapt to specific circumstances. More than the choice of a good method, it is good human and Christian qualities that ensure good success.

73. The advantages of the inductive method, among which the active exercise of spiritual faculties stands out and the continuous reference to concrete reality when explaining difficult concepts, should not lead us to forget the need and usefulness of formulas.
74. a) experience gives rise to interests and questions, hopes and anxieties, reflections and judgments that come together in a certain desire to transform the way of living.

75. All teaching and all true human communication require that an inner activity be made possible and aroused in the one to whom they are addressed. In catechesis, therefore, the activity of faith must be aroused (también de esperanza y caridad); since the righteousness and the capacity for judgment that active teaching must arouse are here at the service of welcoming the Word of God. The optimism about human possibilities, which is typical of all active education, should not make us forget that the act of faith necessarily involves the conversion of the person.
77. There are many ways in which catechesis can convey the Christian message in a manner appropriate to man's circumstances. -

78. The beginnings of religious and moral life are evident from the dawn of human life. In a family of believers, the first months and years of life, which are of particular importance for the balance of the future man, can already provide the conditions for a Christian personality.

79. When the child begins to attend school, he or she becomes part of a society larger than the family, and begins, in an intense way, which absorbs a notable part of his or her energies and interests, life in the society of adults. At school he has his first work experiences (Cf. GE. 5).

80. There are also large and sometimes quite populated regions where school organization is insufficient. In these cases it is necessary to develop intense pastoral work towards families and promote, as far as possible, various associations, appropriately prepared that take care of the children and respond to local conditions and the spiritual needs they have.

81. There is increasing awareness of the difficulty of catechesis aimed at children who live in families or environments where religious practice is lacking or is notably insufficient. Sometimes doubts are heard about the possibility and convenience of this catechesis.

82. The stage of adolescence and, even more so, the "phenomenon of youth" are of crucial importance (Cfr. AA. 12). In pre-industrial societies, with few schools, children moved almost directly from childhood to integration into the adult community. Today, however, the practice of extending the time of school obligation for adolescents prevails; This practice gives rise in society to a generation not integrated into directly productive work, which, although in full physical and intellectual vigor, does not develop any other activity outside of studying and learning the future profession.
83. It is necessary that the National Directories distinguish between pre-adolescence, adolescence and youth.

84. The adolescent notices profound physical and psychological transformations in himself and is searching for his role in society. He is dissatisfied with the religiosity of his childhood but has not yet reached the maturity of faith that is typical of an adult: that is why he seeks a fundamental orientation that can give unity to his life. Many times this search can translate into a religious crisis.

85. The adolescent tries to organize his vision of life and his behavior around some fundamental and primary values. But he notices that he is immersed in a tide of contradictory values. This fact intensifies the adolescent's conflict with the various values ​​and impels him to reject those that he does not see expressed with conviction in the way of life of adults.

88. The adolescent, by himself, has the "formal" use of reasoning. He knows how to use his understanding correctly and discovers that the culture that is proposed to him requires further reflection and concrete application to life.
89. Activity is necessary for the development of the adolescent's personality. Liberation from egocentrism and subjectivism requires contact with reality, whether with its successes or failures.

90. Young people who carry out a job or a profession, and there are many, are led to an accelerated development of their personality. This hasty maturation can come in an orderly or disorderly manner, in a complete or incomplete manner.

91. This duty should not be considered secondary and marginal. Maladjusted children and adolescents do not constitute a small part of the population. The conditions of modern society often make the balanced growth of young people and their adaptation in society difficult.
92. This General Directory strongly affirms the need for adult catechesis for the following reasons:
93. The adult man is ordinarily more capable of communion and mutual relationships with others. -
94. Adulthood is particularly characterized by the awareness of having reached full maturity.
95. The pastoral importance of this period of life is not sufficiently recognized.
96. There are situations and circumstances in which special forms of catechesis are imposed.
97. To respond to the most urgent needs of our time, adult catechesis must:
98. From what has been said about catechetical action and the content of catechesis, a path for pastoral action emerges whose fundamental lines will be examined in this sixth part.
99. It is necessary to have, within the scope of the Episcopal Conference, a clear vision of the situation in which the ministry of the Word is exercised.

100. The object of this investigation is complex. It embraces the examination of pastoral action and the analysis of the religious situation and sociocultural and economic conditions as collective processes that can have profound repercussions on the spread of the Gospel.
101. In this work, which presents notable difficulties, it is necessary above all to point out two dangers:

102. The analysis of the situation is not an end in itself, but it must illuminate the most valid activities and open the way to adopt them, either by increasing the works and initiatives whose effectiveness has been proven, or by promoting new ones. It's really about anticipating and preparing what is necessary for the future.

103. After having explored the situation, it is advisable to proceed to publish a program of action, which can be done through the Catechetical Directory. This Program determines the objectives, the means of catechetical pastoral care and the norms that regulate it, and this in Armenia with the purpose and norms of the universal Church and with a determined fidelity to local needs.

104. Pastoral goals may be different according to places and needs; but all must look towards the progress of faith, the moral commitment of Christians and towards the development of their relationships with God and with men, for example: the access of adults to a mature faith, the insertion of Christian thought in scientific and technical circles, the exercise by the family of its Christian responsibilities, the active presence of Christians in the work of social transformation.

105. The means to be used are above all: the catechetical institutes that must be promoted and supported, the programs, the texts (Cfr. Cap. IV de esta parte), the work instruments and the directives about the methods (-Cfr. parte IV), etc. The scope of media research is practically inexhaustible. However, it is always necessary to carefully check that the proposed means are truly adequate to the spiritual ends to be achieved.

referencias.descripcion: Cfr. Cap. IV de esta parte

contenido: 106. The norms on catechesis can be multiple, they vary according to the purposes to be achieved. Among them, the norms that concern the catechesis of preparation for the sacraments are of particular importance: for example the norms on the catechumenate of adults; on the sacramental initiation of children, on the preparation of families for the Baptism of children.

107. Above all, it is important to make a clear and effective distribution of responsibilities and tasks. It is important, for example, that the responsibilities of Christian families, ecclesial communities, clergy, and catechists be clarified and highlighted. However, we cannot limit ourselves to the pure distribution of existing forces but must promote an ever greater commitment on the part of everyone.

108. Any pastoral activity whose exercise does not involve well-trained people is bound to fail. The same work materials become ineffective if they are not used by well-trained catechists. Catechetical formation, therefore, has priority over the renewal of texts and the improvement of the catechetical organization itself.

109. Higher institutes of catechetical pastoral care must be encouraged and created, in order to prepare catechists qualified to direct catechesis in the diocesan field or in the scope of the activities carried out by religious congregations. These higher institutes may be national or even international in nature. They must be planned like University Institutes, in terms of the organization of studies, the duration of the courses and the conditions for admission.

110. Continuing training includes various modalities and degrees. It is necessary that it be prolonged for the entire time that the catechists dedicate themselves to their specific mission. That is why she looks at both the leaders of catechism and the simple catechists. -

111. The essential purpose of catechetical formation is to enable people to communicate the Christian message. Therefore, a more or less profound theological-doctrinal, anthropological and methodological training is required depending on the scientific level that one wants to achieve. The acquisition of this theoretical knowledge, however, does not exhaust the purposes of the formation which can be called complete - only when the catechist becomes capable of finding in the confrontation of groups and people, in situations that are always peculiar, the most valid way to. transmit the evangelical message. -~

112. a) The doctrine. The need to acquire a valid doctrinal heritage is evident. This includes adequate knowledge of Catholic doctrine, which in higher institutes must reach the level of scientific theology. The Holy Scripture is like the soul of this formation.

113. A specific preparation is required so that the catechist becomes capable of correctly interpreting the reactions of a group or of a person, discovering their spiritual capacity and choosing the way to transmit the evangelical message so that it can be received with true fruit. The methods for such learning are various: practical exercises, teamwork, case analysis, etc.

114. The mission that the catechist is called to carry out requires an intense sacramental and spiritual life, familiarity with prayer, and deep admiration for the greatness of the Christian message and its ability to transform life. But it requires at the same time an emotional desire for charity, humility and prudence that allows the Holy Spirit to carry out its fruitful work in those catechized.
115. It is necessary that ecclesiastical authorities consider the formation of catechists as a task of the utmost importance. -
116. Among the main instruments of catechesis we must list:

117. The purpose of the directories is to promote and coordinate catechetical action in a region or nation or also in many nations belonging to the same sociocultural area. The directories, before being promulgated, must be submitted to the consideration of each of the Ordinaries and to [the approval of the Apostolic See (n. 134).

118. The programs specify, according to age and places and times, the educational goals to be achieved, the methodological principles to be used, and the contents to be transmitted. It is absolutely essential that the mysteries of faith, contained in the creed of adults, are already presented in the catechism programs for children and adolescents in a manner appropriate to their age (Cfr. n. 134).

119. Great importance must be given to the catechisms published by ecclesiastical authority. Its objective is to deliver in a condensed and practical form, the documents of revelation and Christian tradition and the fundamental elements, indispensable to catechetical discourse, that is, to the personal education of the faith. Therefore, due esteem should be given to the documents of tradition and great care should be taken to avoid presenting as belonging to the faith particular interpretations, which are nothing more than personal hypotheses or opinions of some theological school. The doctrine of the Church must be transmitted faithfully.

120. Didactic texts are subsidies or aid offered to the Christian community committed to catechesis. No text can replace the living communication of the Christian message. The texts, however, are very important because they contribute to a more diffuse explanation of the documents of the Christian tradition and the other elements that constitute the catechetical discourse. Also for the writing of these texts, collaborative work is required on the part of the most experts in catechetics and - the consultation of other specialists. -
122. Audiovisual media are mainly used:

123. The most media have the power, among others, to give the character of reality and timeliness to the facts, institutions, and ideas they speak of and, on the contrary, to diminish in common opinion the credit of things that remain silent. -

124. In the area of ​​audiovisual media that catechesis can and should use to better achieve its goals, the didactic method known as "programmed teaching" should not be forgotten, a recent method, but one that is becoming increasingly important.
125. Within the scope of the Episcopal Conference, the organization of catechesis primarily includes diocesan, regional and national structures. -

126. With the decree "Provido Sane", (Cfr. ASS, 1935, p. 151 Sig.) the Diocesan Catechetical Office was established with the aim of presiding over the entire catechetical organization. This job must be made up of a group of people who are truly experts in the field. The breadth and diversity of the issues in which the Catechetical Office must be interested require that responsibilities be distributed among many competent people.

127. It is beneficial for several Dioceses to unite their action, pooling research and activities, capacities and resources, so that the Dioceses with the most supplies come to the aid of the others and a common program of action and regional character can be developed. -
128. It is essential that the Episcopal Conference, and more directly the Episcopal Commission for Catechesis, be assisted by a permanent body.

129. Given that every important act of the Church participates in the ministry of the word and catechesis is always related to the entire ecclesial life, it is necessary that catechetical activity be coordinated with general pastoral care. The purpose of this cooperation is the harmonious development of the Christian community that, even within the specific context of each function, pursues a single fundamental purpose.

130. The catechumenate of adults, which is at the same time catechesis, liturgical participation and community life, is the typical case of an institution that is born from the collaboration of various pastoral activities; Its purpose is to guide the spiritual itinerary, the change of mentality and customs of those who prepare for Baptism. It is a preparatory school for Christian life, it is an introduction to the religious, liturgical, charitable and apostolic life of the people of God (Cfr. AG. 13-14; SC. 65; CD. 14). The entire Christian community, through the godparents who represent it, and not only priests or catechists, is committed to this work.
131. Without scientific research the catechetical movement would be paralyzed, given the rapid evolution of the culture of our times.

132. The Apostolic College is supportive in the exercise of its mission (Cfr. LG. 22-23; AG. 38; CD 2,4). Many times in this part of the Directory the consequences that follow from this solidarity in regard to catechesis have been indicated (por ejemplo el Capítulo II: armonización de las metas pastorales de las naciones vecinas; Cap. III: creación de Institutos Superiores; Cap. IV: elaboración de instrumentos comunes de trabajo; Cap. VII: investigación científica).

referencias.descripcion: por ejemplo el Capítulo II: armonización de las metas pastorales de las naciones vecinas; Cap. III: creación de Institutos Superiores; Cap. IV: elaboración de instrumentos comunes de trabajo; Cap. VII: investigación científica

contenido: 133. As 'Peter was constituted head of the Apostolic College and foundation of the Church, so the successor of Peter, that is, the Roman Pontiff, (Cfr. LG, 22), is the visible head of the Episcopal College and of all the people of God. He fulfills his obligation of teaching and government as Vicar of Christ and Pastor of the entire Church (LG, 22) always for the spiritual good of the People of God and for its growth. He can exercise his function according to the needs of the Church with complete freedom in various ways, that is, either personally or collegially, that is together with the Bishops of the entire Church.

134. The central responsibility for catechesis for the common law territories is entrusted to the Sacred Congregation for the Clergy (Oficio Segundo). She has the task of stimulating, coordinating and guiding everything that concerns the preaching of the Word of God and the works of apostolate; to spread the news and promote, as far as possible, cooperation between the various nations. -
